subQuestions.questionText:
The information below is for a South African Airways flight from Cape Town to Johannesburg.

| SOUTH AFRICAN AIRWAYS – Wednesday 8 January 2025 | |
|---|---|
| Distance | 1 278 km |
| Aircraft | Boeing 737-800 |
| Codeshare | NZ 3120 |
| Flight number | SA332 |
| Maximum number of passengers | 189 |
| Departure | 12:15 Cape Town |
| Arrival | 14:15 Johannesburg |

State, in words, the arrival time of the flight using the 12-hour format.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: Quarter past two in the afternoon (1RT correct time in words; 1A correct time of day)

OR

Fifteen minutes after two in the afternoon (1RT correct time in words; 1A correct time of day)

Teaching point: Two marks means TWO pieces of information are wanted — the time itself (quarter past two) AND the time of day (in the afternoon / p.m.). Writing only 'quarter past two' loses the second mark. Convert 24-hour to 12-hour by subtracting 12 from any hour greater than 12: $14:15 - 12 = 2{:}15$ p.m.

subQuestions.questionText:
The information below is for a South African Airways flight from Cape Town to Johannesburg.

| SOUTH AFRICAN AIRWAYS – Wednesday 8 January 2025 | |
|---|---|
| Distance | 1 278 km |
| Aircraft | Boeing 737-800 |
| Codeshare | NZ 3120 |
| Flight number | SA332 |
| Maximum number of passengers | 189 |
| Departure | 12:15 Cape Town |
| Arrival | 14:15 Johannesburg |

Only $33\dfrac{1}{3}\%$ of the maximum number of passengers were on board this flight.

Calculate the number of passengers on this flight.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\text{Number of passengers} = 33\dfrac{1}{3}\% \times 189$ (1MA multiplying by $33\frac{1}{3}\%$)
Mark 2: $= 63$ (1A simplification)

OR

Mark 1: $\text{Number of passengers} = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 189$ (1MA multiplying by $\frac{1}{3}$)
Mark 2: $= 63$ (1A simplification)

Teaching point: $33\frac{1}{3}\%$ is exactly $\frac{1}{3}$. Using the fraction is quicker and avoids rounding errors that come from typing 33,33% into a calculator.

subQuestions.questionText:
The information below is for a South African Airways flight from Cape Town to Johannesburg.

| SOUTH AFRICAN AIRWAYS – Wednesday 8 January 2025 | |
|---|---|
| Distance | 1 278 km |
| Aircraft | Boeing 737-800 |
| Codeshare | NZ 3120 |
| Flight number | SA332 |
| Maximum number of passengers | 189 |
| Departure | 12:15 Cape Town |
| Arrival | 14:15 Johannesburg |

Write down which ONE of the methods below is the CORRECT method to calculate the speed in km/h of the aircraft.

Write only the letter (A–C).

A  $\dfrac{1\,278}{14{:}15}$

B  $\dfrac{1\,278}{2}$

C  $\dfrac{2}{1\,278}$
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: B (2A correct letter)

Teaching point: $\text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$. The distance is 1 278 km and the TIME TAKEN is $14{:}15 - 12{:}15 = 2$ hours — not the clock reading 14:15. So the correct expression is $\dfrac{1\,278}{2} = 639$ km/h. Option A wrongly uses the arrival clock time and option C turns the formula upside down.

subQuestions.questionText:
A South African Airways flight (SA332) from Cape Town to Johannesburg took place on Wednesday 8 January 2025.

State which day of the week was 26 December 2024.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: Thursday (2A correct day)

Teaching point: Work backwards in 7-day steps from a day you know. 8 January 2025 is a Wednesday, so 1 January 2025 is also a Wednesday (7 days earlier). December 2024 has 31 days, so 31 December 2024 is a Tuesday, and counting back: 30 Dec = Monday, 29 Dec = Sunday, 28 Dec = Saturday, 27 Dec = Friday, 26 Dec = Thursday.

subQuestions.questionText:
One way to save money during winter is to wrap the geyser and waterpipes with a geyser blanket. A geyser blanket is made of aerolite, an insulating material that keeps heat inside an object and which can easily be cut.

Six pictures, labelled P to U, show the steps for wrapping a geyser in aerolite. They are printed in two rows of three: the TOP row, read from left to right, is P, Q, R, and the BOTTOM row, read from left to right, is U, T, S. The arrows run P → Q → R across the top row, then turn down at the right-hand end onto S, and then run from right to left along the bottom row: S → T → U. The pictures show the following:

| Picture | What the picture shows |
|---|---|
| P | A man kneeling next to the cylindrical geyser (lying on its side), unrolling a large sheet of aerolite and wrapping it around the curved side of the geyser |
| Q | The man leaning over the now-covered geyser, pulling a long strip of sticky tape tightly around the outside of the wrapped curved surface |
| R | The man bending over a flat sheet of aerolite lying on the floor, cutting a circular shape out of the sheet (the faint outline of a circle is drawn on the sheet) |
| S | The man kneeling and running a glue applicator across the face of a round piece of aerolite that he is holding |
| T | The man pressing a round piece of aerolite onto the flat circular end of the wrapped geyser |
| U | A close-up of a pair of hands winding a narrow strip of aerolite around a water pipe, part of the pipe already being covered |

Write down the letter (P–U) of the picture that matches EACH of the following statements:

(a) Cut out circles of the aerolite to be placed on both ends of the geyser.
(b) Apply glue to the circular pieces of the aerolite.
(c) The strips of aerolite are wrapped around the pipes.
(d) Roll the aerolite around the lateral surface of the geyser.
(e) Use duct tape to secure the aerolite around the lateral surface.
(f) Attach the circular pieces of the aerolite to the geyser.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) R (1A correct letter)
(b) S (1A correct letter)
(c) U (1A correct letter)
(d) P (1A correct letter)
(e) Q (1A correct letter)
(f) T (1A correct letter)

Teaching point: A geyser is a CYLINDER. Its 'lateral surface' is the curved side (a rectangle when unrolled) and its two ends are CIRCLES. That is why the aerolite is first rolled around the curved side and taped, and then two separate circles are cut, glued and stuck onto the ends.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Surface area of a cylinder in context

subQuestions.questionText:
A geyser is a closed cylinder. It is wrapped in aerolite: a rectangular sheet is rolled around the curved (lateral) surface and a circle of aerolite is glued to each of the two flat circular ends.

Choose ONE of the following formulae that can be used to calculate how much aerolite is needed for the total surface area of the geyser only.

Write only the letter (A–D).

A  $\pi \times \text{radius}^2 \times \text{height} + 2 \times \pi \times \text{radius}$

B  $\pi \times \text{radius} \times \text{height} + \text{length} \times \text{width}$

C  $2 \times \pi \times \text{radius} \times \text{height} + 2 \times \pi \times \text{radius}^2$

D  $\dfrac{1}{2}\text{base} \times \text{height}$
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: C (2A correct formula)

Teaching point: Total surface area of a closed cylinder $= 2\pi r h + 2\pi r^2$. The first term $2\pi r h$ is the curved side (its width is the circumference $2\pi r$ and its height is $h$); the second term $2\pi r^2$ is the TWO circular ends. Option A is the volume formula muddled with a circumference; option D is the area of a triangle.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Surface area formula of a cylinder

subQuestions.questionText:
A geyser is to be wrapped in aerolite. The length of the geyser is 1,2 m.

Convert this measurement to mm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\text{Length of geyser} = 1{,}2 \text{ m} \times 1\,000$ (1MA multiplying by 1 000)
Mark 2: $= 1\,200 \text{ mm}$ (1A conversion)

Teaching point: $1 \text{ m} = 1\,000 \text{ mm}$. Going from a BIGGER unit (m) to a SMALLER unit (mm) means the number must get bigger, so you multiply.

questions.title: Tourist bus seating plan, a Cape Town tour route map and floor plans of two flats

subQuestions.questionText:
The seating plan for a double-decker tourist bus that travels around Cape Town shows the following:

| Deck | Rows | Seats shown |
|---|---|---|
| UPPER DECK | Rows G to V | 59 seats |
| LOWER DECK | Rows A to F | 22 seats AND the driver seat |

The KEY on the plan shows four symbols: driver seat, toilet, forward-facing seat and stairs. Every passenger seat drawn on the plan is a forward-facing seat EXCEPT for FOUR seats near the front of the LOWER deck (two on each side of the aisle), which are drawn facing the back of the bus. The driver seat is not a passenger seat.

Determine the number of forward-facing passenger seats on this bus.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\text{Number of seats} = 59 + 22 - 4$ (1MA addition and subtraction of the correct values)
Mark 2: $= 77 \text{ seats}$ (1A simplification)

Answer only: full marks.

Teaching point: Add the seats on BOTH decks first ($59 + 22 = 81$ passenger seats) and only then take away the 4 seats that are not forward-facing. The driver seat is already excluded from the 22, so do not subtract it again.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading a seating plan

subQuestions.questionText:
A double-decker tourist bus in Cape Town has the following seating plan:

- LOWER DECK: 22 seats plus the driver seat. The driver seat is at the very front of the bus. The lower-deck seating rows run from row A (nearest the front of the bus) to row F (the last row of the lower deck).
- UPPER DECK: 59 seats in rows G (nearest the front) to V (the very back of the bus).
- The toilet is on the LOWER DECK. It is at the rear end of the lower-deck cabin, on the left-hand side of the bus, and its door opens onto the aisle right next to row F.

The seats are numbered according to the following numbering system:

- A to F is for the lower deck.
- G to V is for the upper deck.
- The seats are numbered 1 to 4 from right to left if you are facing the back of the bus.

Write down the seat number which has the easiest access to the toilet.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: F2 (1A correct row; 1A correct seat)

Teaching point: Answer in two steps. (1) The ROW: the toilet is on the lower deck at the rear of the cabin, so the nearest row is F. (2) The SEAT: a passenger reaches the toilet by walking down the AISLE, so the aisle seat on the toilet side is the easiest — seat 2. Together that gives F2.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Seating plan and position

subQuestions.questionText:
A double-decker tourist bus in Cape Town has the following seating plan:

- LOWER DECK: rows A (nearest the front of the bus) to F (last row of the lower deck), 22 seats plus the driver seat at the very front.
- UPPER DECK: rows G (nearest the front) to V (the very back), 59 seats.
- There are TWO sets of stairs joining the decks: a FRONT set near the front of the bus and a rear set. On the plan the FRONT set of stairs is drawn on the RIGHT-HAND side of the bus; on the upper deck it takes the place of the seats in row H.
- The seats are numbered 1 to 4 from right to left if you are facing the back of the bus, so seats 1 and 2 are on the bus's left-hand side (1 at the window, 2 on the aisle) and seats 3 and 4 are on the bus's right-hand side (3 on the aisle, 4 at the window).
- Counting backwards from the front set of stairs along the upper deck, row J is the SECOND row.

Complete the following paragraph with the directions to move from seat C2 to seat J3, by using the words provided in the list below. Write only the word next to the question numbers (a) to (d).

Word list: aisle;  second;  left;  right;  first

'Move forward towards the front set of stairs on your (a) … Use this set of stairs to get to the upper deck. Once on the upper deck, turn (b) … and you will find your seat on the (c) … in the (d) … row from the stairs.'
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Right (1A correct choice)
(b) Left (1A correct choice)
(c) Aisle (1A correct choice)
(d) Second (1A correct choice)

Teaching point: Directions on a plan are always given from the point of view of the PERSON WALKING, not from the reader looking down at the page. Seat C2 is on the bus's left-hand side; walking forward (facing the front of the bus) puts the front stairs on that person's right. At the top of the stairs the passenger turns to face the back of the bus, which puts the bus’s right-hand side — where seat 3 sits, on the aisle — on the passenger’s left, two rows along.

subQuestions.questionText:
A route map shows a round trip made by a tour bus in Cape Town, together with the 18 stops the bus makes. The stops are numbered 1 to 18 in the order in which the bus visits them, and north is at the top of the map. The route forms a closed loop that starts and ends at the V&A Waterfront: from stops 1 and 2 at the Waterfront it works through the city centre (CTICC, cathedral, museums, Castle of Good Hope), out to the Table Mountain Cableway at stop 13, down the Atlantic seaboard to Camps Bay at stop 14, and then back north along the coast through Sea Point and Green Point to the Waterfront.

Of all 18 stops printed on the map, the stop that lies lowest on the map — that is, the furthest SOUTH — is the stop labelled Camps Bay.

Write down the name of the southern-most stop on this route.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: Camps Bay (2RT correct stop)

Teaching point: On a standard map north is at the top, so 'southern-most' means the point printed LOWEST on the page. Check the compass direction indicator before deciding which way is south.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Compass directions on a map

subQuestions.questionText:
A route map shows a round trip made by a tour bus in Cape Town and the 18 stops on the route.

The scale on this map is NOT written as a ratio such as 1 : 50 000. Instead it is drawn as a short measured line, divided into blocks and labelled with the real distance it represents: on this map a drawn bar 13 mm (1,3 cm) long is labelled '500 m'.

Name the type of scale used on this map.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: Bar scale / Line scale / Linear scale / Graphic scale (2RT correct scale — any one of these names)

Teaching point: There are only TWO types of scale in Mathematical Literacy. A NUMBER scale is written as a ratio (e.g. $1:50\,000$). A BAR scale is a drawn, measured line labelled with the real distance. A bar scale stays correct even if the map is enlarged or reduced on a photocopier, which is why maps in guidebooks usually use it.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Types of scale

subQuestions.questionText:
A route map shows a round trip made by a tour bus in Cape Town, with the 18 stops numbered 1 to 18 in the order in which the bus visits them. North is at the top of the map and the route forms a closed loop.

On the map, stops 11 to 18 lie on the return part of the loop. Following the numbers in order from stop 11 through to stop 18, the bus travels around the loop turning in the SAME sense as the hands of a clock move on a clock face.

State whether the bus will be driving in a clockwise or an anticlockwise direction from stop 11 to stop 18.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: Clockwise (2A correct direction)

Teaching point: To decide the direction of travel on a circular route, put your finger on the first stop number and trace to the next numbers in order. If your finger moves the way clock hands move (top → right → bottom → left), the direction is clockwise; the opposite is anticlockwise.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Direction of travel

subQuestions.questionText:
A route map shows a round trip made by a tour bus in Cape Town.

The map has a BAR SCALE printed on it. When measured with a ruler, the bar on the map is 13 mm (1,3 cm) long, and it is labelled 500 m. (An accepted measurement of 12 mm is also allowed.)

The distance of a round trip is 19,2 km.

Use the given scale on the map to determine the map distance.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: measured bar $= 13 \text{ mm}$ (1A measured distance)
Mark 2: $13 \text{ mm} = 500 \text{ m}$ (1RT correct ratio)
Mark 3: real distance in metres: $19{,}2 \text{ km} = 19\,200 \text{ m}$ (1C convert to m)
Mark 4: map distance $= 19\,200 \div 500 \times 13$ (1MCA dividing and multiplying)
Mark 5: $= 499{,}2 \text{ mm}$ (1CA simplification)

OR

Mark 1: bar $= 1{,}3 \text{ cm}$ (1A measured distance)
Mark 2: $1{,}3 \text{ cm} = 500 \text{ m}$ (1RT correct ratio)
Mark 3: $500 \text{ m} = 0{,}5 \text{ km}$ (1C convert to km)
Mark 4: map distance $= \dfrac{19{,}2 \text{ km} \times 1{,}3 \text{ cm}}{0{,}5 \text{ km}}$ (1MCA dividing and multiplying)
Mark 5: $= 49{,}92 \text{ cm}$ (1CA simplification)

OR (using a number scale)

Mark 1: measured bar $= 1{,}3 \text{ cm}$ (1A)
Mark 2: $1{,}3 \text{ cm} : 500 \text{ m}$ (1RT correct ratio)
Mark 3: $0{,}013 \text{ m} : 500 \text{ m}$, i.e. $1 : 38\,461{,}53846$ (1C convert to m)
Mark 4: $? = \dfrac{19{,}2}{38\,461{,}53846}$ (1MCA dividing by the scale factor)
Mark 5: $= 0{,}0004992 \text{ km} = 49{,}92 \text{ cm}$ OR $499{,}2 \text{ mm}$ (1CA simplification)

NOTE: a measurement of 12 mm is accepted, giving 460,8 mm.

Teaching point: With a bar scale, always work in the SAME unit on both sides first. Find how many 'bar lengths' fit into the real distance ($19\,200 \div 500 = 38{,}4$) and then multiply by the length of one bar ($38{,}4 \times 13 \text{ mm} = 499{,}2 \text{ mm}$).
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Bar scale calculations

subQuestions.questionText:
John lives in a flat in Cape Town. Floor plans are given for two flats in his block: Flat 1 is on the ground floor and Flat 2 is on the first floor.

On both floor plans each door is drawn in the usual way — a straight line for the door leaf together with a quarter-circle arc showing the direction in which the door swings open. On the bathroom doorway the arc is drawn so that, as you walk through the doorway INTO the bathroom, the door leaf swings away from you towards your right-hand side.

State whether the bathroom door opens to the (left/right) as you enter the bathroom.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: Right (2A correct direction)

Teaching point: On a floor plan a door is drawn as a line plus a quarter-circle 'swing' arc. Imagine yourself standing in the doorway facing the direction you would walk — the side on which the arc is drawn tells you which way the door opens. Left and right are always from the point of view of the PERSON WALKING IN, not from the reader looking down at the plan.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading a floor plan

subQuestions.questionText:
John lives in a flat in Cape Town. The floor plan of his flat is labelled in imperial units (feet and inches). The living room on the plan is labelled with two dimensions, and the LONGER of the two is 12'8" (that is, 12 feet 8 inches).

Use the conversions 1 foot = 30,48 cm and 1 inch = 2,54 cm.

Convert the longer dimension of the living room to centimetres.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: longer dimension $= 12'8"$ (1RT reading 12'8" from the plan)
Mark 2: $12' \times 30{,}48$ (1MCA multiplying by 30,48)
Mark 3: $= 365{,}76 \text{ cm}$ (1C converting feet to cm)
Mark 4: $8" \times 2{,}54 = 20{,}32 \text{ cm}$ (1C converting inches to cm)
Mark 5: $\text{Total} = 365{,}76 + 20{,}32 = 386{,}08 \text{ cm}$ (1CA simplification)

OR

Mark 1: longer dimension $= 12'8"$ (1RT)
Marks 2–5: $\text{Length} = (12 \times 30{,}48 \text{ cm}) + (8 \times 2{,}54 \text{ cm}) = 365{,}76 \text{ cm} + 20{,}32 \text{ cm} = 386{,}08 \text{ cm}$ (1MCA multiplying by 30,48; 1C feet to cm; 1C inches to cm; 1CA simplification)

Teaching point: The notation $12'8"$ means 12 FEET and 8 INCHES — the apostrophe is feet and the double quote is inches. Convert the two parts SEPARATELY (feet using 30,48 cm and inches using 2,54 cm) and only then add. A common error is to read it as 12,8 feet.

subQuestions.questionText:
John lives in a block of flats in Cape Town. Floor plans are given for two of the flats: Flat 1 is on the GROUND floor and Flat 2 is on the FIRST floor.

The rooms and features shown on the two floor plans are:

| Room / feature | Flat 1 (ground floor) | Flat 2 (first floor) |
|---|---|---|
| Bedroom 13'0" × 10'0" | Yes — two of them | Yes — two of them |
| Bath 6'6" × 5'0" | Yes | Yes |
| Kitchen 6'6" × 7'8" | Yes | Yes |
| Dining room 13'4" × 13'1" | Yes | Yes |
| The room measuring 12'8" × 12'7" | labelled LIVING ROOM | labelled BEDROOM (a third bedroom) |
| Balcony | No | Yes |
| Windows in the north- and south-facing walls | None | None |

Write down TWO differences between Flat 1 and Flat 2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Difference 1 (Marks 1 & 2): One has a living room and the other one has a bedroom (2RT identify first difference)
Difference 2 (Marks 3 & 4): The balcony is on the first floor — Flat 2 has a balcony and Flat 1 does not (2RT identify second difference)

Teaching point: A 'difference' must be a statement about BOTH plans, not just a fact about one. Compare the plans room by room and say what one has that the other does not.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Comparing floor plans

subQuestions.questionText:
John lives in a block of flats in Cape Town. Two floor plans are given: Flat 1 is on the GROUND floor and Flat 2 is on the FIRST floor. Flat 2's plan shows a balcony; Flat 1's plan does not show a balcony.

Give ONE possible reason why Flat 1 does not have a balcony.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: It is on the ground floor (2O explanation)

Accept any equivalent explanation, e.g. a ground-floor flat opens straight onto the ground/garden, so a raised balcony would serve no purpose (and would be a security risk).

Teaching point: A balcony is a raised platform projecting from an UPPER storey. A ground-floor flat is already at ground level, so there is nothing for a balcony to be raised above.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Interpreting a floor plan

subQuestions.questionText:
John lives in a block of flats in Cape Town. Two floor plans are given: Flat 1 (ground floor) and Flat 2 (first floor). Both plans include a compass direction indicator. On BOTH plans all the windows are drawn in the east-facing and west-facing walls — there is not a single window drawn in the north-facing wall or the south-facing wall of either flat.

Explain why there are no windows in the north- and south-facing walls of both plans.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: There must be more flats adjacent to it (2O explanation)

Accept any equivalent explanation, e.g. the north and south walls are shared (party) walls between neighbouring flats in the block, so a window there would look into the flat next door.

Teaching point: A block of flats is a row of units joined side by side. Where two flats share a wall you cannot put a window — windows can only go in the outside (exterior) walls. Reading the compass indicator tells you which walls those are.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Interpreting a floor plan

questions.title: A recycled tree decoration template and circular-shaped earrings

subQuestions.questionText:
Mrs Xulu used different recycled materials to make a tree decoration to hang on the wall. She cut out different coloured circles to form the tree pattern.

Mrs Xulu took 3 hours and 27 minutes without any break to cut out the circles. She finished at 13:12.

Determine the time at which Mrs Xulu started cutting out the circles.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $13{:}12 - 3 \text{ hours and } 27 \text{ min}$ (1MA subtracting time)
Mark 2: $= 09{:}45$ (1A simplification)

OR

Mark 1: $\text{Time} = 13{,}2 - 3{,}45 = 9{,}75 \text{ hours}$ (1MA subtracting the hours)
Mark 2: $= 09{:}45$ (1A simplification)

Answer only: full marks.

Teaching point: When subtracting time, subtract the hours and the minutes separately and 'borrow' 60 minutes if needed: $12 \text{ min} - 27 \text{ min}$ is negative, so borrow an hour → $72 \text{ min} - 27 \text{ min} = 45 \text{ min}$, and $12\text{h} - 3\text{h} = 9\text{h}$, giving 09:45.

subQuestions.questionText:
Mrs Xulu made a tree-shaped cardboard template made up of three sections: Part A (the top triangle), Part B (the middle section) and Part C (the bottom section). Coloured circles are pasted onto the template.

In Part A, there are seven rows of circles. The first row consists of one circle at the top and thereafter, each successive row has an additional circle added to complete the rest of the rows.

Calculate the total number of circles in Part A.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: interpreting the pattern as $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7$ (1RT interpreting the pattern)
Mark 2: adding the values (1MA adding values)
Mark 3: $= 28$ (1CA simplification)

OR

Mark 1: $\text{Number} = \dfrac{7(1+7)}{2}$ (1RT interpreting the pattern)
Mark 2: $= 7 \times 4$ (1MA multiplication of values)
Mark 3: $= 28$ (1CA simplification)

Answer only: full marks.

Teaching point: Row 1 has 1 circle, row 2 has 2, and so on up to row 7 which has 7. Write the rows out and add them, or use the shortcut $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ with $n = 7$.

subQuestions.questionText:
Mrs Xulu made a tree-shaped cardboard template made up of three sections: Part A, Part B and Part C.

Part A is the triangle at the top of the tree. On the template:

| Dimension of Part A | Value |
|---|---|
| Height of the triangle | 240 mm |
| Base of the triangle | 28 cm |

Calculate, in cm², the area of Part A.

You may use the following formula:

Area of triangle $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\text{Height} = 240 \text{ mm} = 24 \text{ cm}$ (1C conversion)
Mark 2: base $= 28$ cm read from the template (1RT 28)
Mark 3: $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}(28 \text{ cm} \times 24 \text{ cm})$ (1SF substitution into the formula)
Mark 4: $= 336 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA simplification)

OR

Mark 1: $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 280 \text{ mm} \times 240 \text{ mm}$ (1SF substitution; 1RT 280)
Mark 2: $= 33\,600 \text{ mm}^2$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 3: $= 336 \text{ cm}^2$ (1C conversion)

Teaching point: The answer must be in cm², so convert the height to cm BEFORE substituting ($240 \text{ mm} \div 10 = 24 \text{ cm}$). If you work in mm² instead, remember that $1 \text{ cm}^2 = 100 \text{ mm}^2$, so you divide by 100 (not 10) at the end.

subQuestions.questionText:
Mrs Xulu's tree-shaped cardboard template is made up of three sections: Part A (the top triangle), Part B (the middle section) and Part C (the bottom section).

| Part | Area |
|---|---|
| Part A | 336 cm² (calculated in QUESTION 3.1.3) |
| Part B | 30 240 mm² |
| Part C | 1,6 times the area of Part B |

Calculate, in mm², the total area of the cardboard template.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\text{Area of C} = 30\,240 \text{ mm}^2 \times 1{,}6$ (1MA multiplying by 1,6)
Mark 2: $= 48\,384 \text{ mm}^2$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 3: $336 \text{ cm}^2 = 33\,600 \text{ mm}^2$ (1C converting to mm²)
Mark 4: $\text{Total area} = 48\,384 \text{ mm}^2 + 30\,240 \text{ mm}^2 + 33\,600 \text{ mm}^2$ (1MCA adding the values)
Mark 5: $= 112\,224 \text{ mm}^2$ (1CA simplification)

OR (working in cm² first)

Part B: $30\,240 \text{ mm}^2 \div 10^2 = 302{,}4 \text{ cm}^2$
Part C: $302{,}4 \text{ cm}^2 \times 1{,}6 = 483{,}84 \text{ cm}^2$ (1MA multiplying by 1,6; 1CA simplification)
Total: $(336 + 483{,}84 + 302{,}4) \text{ cm}^2 = 1\,122{,}24 \text{ cm}^2$ (1MCA adding values; 1CA simplification)
$1\,122{,}24 \times 100 = 112\,224 \text{ mm}^2$ (1C converting to mm²)

CA applies from QUESTION 3.1.3.

Teaching point: For AREA conversions the factor is squared: $1 \text{ cm}^2 = 10 \times 10 = 100 \text{ mm}^2$. So $336 \text{ cm}^2 \times 100 = 33\,600 \text{ mm}^2$. Multiplying by only 10 is the most common mistake in this question.

subQuestions.questionText:
Mrs Xulu placed all the coloured circles she cut out into a container.

TABLE 2: NUMBER OF CIRCLES PER COLOUR

| COLOUR OF CIRCLE | NUMBER OF CIRCLES |
|---|---|
| Red | 9 |
| Green | 7 |
| Gold | 28 |
| Dark denim | 8 |
| Mixed colour | 22 |

Determine, as a percentage, the probability of randomly choosing a green circle or a red circle from the container.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $9 + 7 + 28 + 8 + 22 = 74$ (1A correct total number of circles)
Mark 2: numerator $= 9 + 7 = 16$ (1MA correct numerator)
Mark 3: $P = \dfrac{16}{74} \times 100\%$ (1MA percentage concept)
Mark 4: $\approx 21{,}62\%$ (1CA simplification)

OR

$9 + 7 + 28 + 8 + 22 = 74$ (1A)
$P(\text{red}) = \dfrac{9}{74} \times 100\% = 12{,}16216216\%$ (1MA)
$P(\text{green}) = \dfrac{7}{74} \times 100\% = 9{,}459459459\%$ (1MA)
$P(\text{red or green}) \approx 12{,}16\% + 9{,}46\% = 21{,}62\%$ (1CA)

OR

$9 + 7 + 28 + 8 + 22 = 74$ (1A)
$P(\text{red or green}) = \dfrac{9}{74} + \dfrac{7}{74}$ (1MA; 1MA)
$= 0{,}216216\ldots \times 100\% = 21{,}62\%$ (1CA)

Teaching point: 'A green circle OR a red circle' means the two favourable groups are ADDED, because a circle cannot be both green and red at the same time (mutually exclusive events). Always work out the TOTAL of all the circles first — it is the denominator.

subQuestions.questionText:
Amanda Xulu makes circular-shaped earrings which she sells at the local flea market. Each earring is made from a SMALL circle joined above a LARGE circle.

The radius of the large circle is 14 mm.

Determine, in mm, the radius of the small circle if it is $\dfrac{4}{7}$ of the radius of the large circle.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\text{Radius of small circle} = \dfrac{4}{7} \times 14 \text{ mm}$ (1MA multiplying by 14)
Mark 2: $= 8 \text{ mm}$ (1A correct length)

Answer only: full marks.

Teaching point: 'Of' means MULTIPLY. Divide 14 by the denominator 7 first ($14 \div 7 = 2$) and then multiply by the numerator 4 ($2 \times 4 = 8$) — that keeps the numbers small and avoids decimals.
subQuestions.topic: Number sense – Fraction of a quantity

subQuestions.questionText:
Amanda Xulu makes circular-shaped earrings. Each earring has a large circle with a radius of 14 mm.

Calculate, rounded to the nearest mm, the circumference of the large circle.

You may use the following formula:

Circumference of circle $= 3{,}142 \times 2 \times \text{radius}$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\text{Circumference} = 3{,}142 \times 2 \times 14 \text{ mm}$ (1SF substitution into the formula)
Mark 2: $= 87{,}976 \text{ mm}$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 3: $\approx 88 \text{ mm}$ (1R rounding)

Teaching point: Rounding is an INDEPENDENT mark in this paper, so it is worth a mark on its own — always finish the question by rounding as the instruction asks. 'Nearest mm' means a whole number of millimetres, so 87,976 rounds up to 88 mm.

subQuestions.questionText:
Amanda Xulu decides to make 48 PAIRS of earrings using flower-patterned synthetic leather for the LARGE circles. Both sides of each large circle are covered using synthetic leather, while the small circle is painted black.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Radius of one large circle | 1,4 cm |
| Width of the roll of synthetic leather | 1,37 m |
| Length of synthetic leather Amanda buys | 30 cm |
| Number of PAIRS of earrings | 48 |

She states that after cutting the leather for ALL the large circles, the remaining synthetic leather will have an area of less than 3 000 cm².

Verify her statement, showing ALL calculations.

You may use the following formulae:

Area of rectangle $= \text{length} \times \text{width}$

Area of circle $= 3{,}142 \times \text{radius}^2$
subQuestions.memoText:
Area of material:
Mark 1: $1{,}37 \text{ m} = 137 \text{ cm}$ (1C converting to cm)
Mark 2: $\text{Area} = 30 \text{ cm} \times 137 \text{ cm}$ (1SF substitution into the formula)
Mark 3: $= 4\,110 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA correct area)

Total area of all the circles:
Mark 4: $= 3{,}142 \times (1{,}4 \text{ cm})^2 \times 48 \times 2 \times 2$ (1SF substitution into the formula)
Mark 5: $\times 48$ (1MA multiplying by 48)
Mark 6: $\times 2 \times 2$ (1MA multiplying by $2 \times 2$ — two earrings per pair, two sides per earring)
Mark 7: $= 1\,182{,}40 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA simplification)

Area of off-cuts:
Mark 8: $= 4\,110 \text{ cm}^2 - 1\,182{,}40 \text{ cm}^2 = 2\,927{,}60 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA area of off-cuts)
Mark 9: $2\,927{,}60 \text{ cm}^2 < 3\,000 \text{ cm}^2$, so her statement is CORRECT (1O opinion)

OR

$\text{Area of material} = 30 \text{ cm} \times 137 \text{ cm} = 4\,110 \text{ cm}^2$ (1C; 1SF; 1CA)
$\text{Area of one circle} = 3{,}142 \times (1{,}4 \text{ cm})^2 = 6{,}15832 \text{ cm}^2$ (1SF)
$\text{Number of circles} = 48 \times 2 = 96$ (1MA multiplying by 48)
$\text{For both sides} = 96 \times 2 = 192$ (1MA multiplying 96 by 2)
$\text{Total area} = 6{,}15832 \text{ cm}^2 \times 192 = 1\,182{,}39744 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA)
$\text{Off-cuts} = 4\,110 - 1\,182{,}39744 \approx 2\,927{,}60 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA)
Her statement is CORRECT (1O)

Teaching point: Read the counting carefully — 48 PAIRS means $48 \times 2 = 96$ large circles, and BOTH SIDES of each are covered, so $96 \times 2 = 192$ leather circles in total. Also convert the roll width 1,37 m to 137 cm so that both dimensions of the rectangle are in the same unit before multiplying.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Area of circles and rectangles (verification)

questions.title: Tracking a flamingo's flight across a road map of South Africa

subQuestions.questionText:
A flamingo (bird) was fitted with a Global Positioning System (GPS) tracking device. A road map shows the tracked flight of the flamingo across the central interior of South Africa, starting at point A and ending at point E. North is at the top of the map.

The map shows towns, national roads (each numbered inside a pentagon) and provincial borders. Among the towns marked are Kimberley, Britstown, De Aar, Hanover, Colesberg, Middelburg and Queenstown.

Reading due WEST from Colesberg along the same line of latitude, the first (nearest) town shown on the map is De Aar, with Britstown lying further west beyond it.

Name the closest town directly west of Colesberg.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: De Aar (2A correct town)

Teaching point: 'Directly west' means straight across the map to the LEFT of Colesberg, keeping the same height on the page — not simply the nearest town in any direction. Use the compass indicator on the map before you decide.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Compass directions on a map

subQuestions.label: 4.1.2 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
A road map shows the GPS-tracked flight of a flamingo across the central interior of South Africa, from point A to point E.

National roads are indicated with a number enclosed in a pentagon, e.g. a pentagon containing the number 1 means the N1.

On this map the following different pentagon route markers appear: N1, N2, N5, N6, N8, N9, N10 and N12. Several of them are printed more than once, at different places along the same road. (The map also carries an “A2” marker drawn in a rectangle, not in a pentagon, so it is not a national road.)

Write down how many different national roads are shown on this map.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: 8 (2A correct number)

Teaching point: Count each national road ONCE, no matter how many pentagon markers of the same number appear along its length. The N1, for example, may be marked at several places along the route but is still only ONE national road.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading map symbols

subQuestions.label: 4.1.2 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
A road map shows the GPS-tracked flight of a flamingo across the central interior of South Africa. National roads are indicated with a number enclosed in a pentagon (e.g. a pentagon containing 12 means the N12).

The towns printed on this map are Kimberley, Douglas, Orania, Britstown, De Aar, Colesberg, Hanover, Middelburg, Nieu Bethesda, Graaff-Reinet, Bloemfontein, Botshabelo, Aliwal North, Queenstown, Makhanda and Port Alfred. The N12 runs south-westwards across the map, and the only two of these towns that lie ON the N12 are Kimberley and Britstown.

Name the towns found on the N12.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: Kimberley (2A first correct town)
Mark 3: Britstown (1A second correct town)

Teaching point: Trace the N12 line with your finger from one edge of the map to the other and write down EVERY town the line passes through. Note the penalty rule for this paper: if you list extra towns that are not on the N12, you are penalised for each extra item.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading a road map

subQuestions.questionText:
A road map shows the GPS-tracked flight of a flamingo across the central interior of South Africa. The map shows towns, national roads and the boundaries between provinces.

On this map the national roads are drawn as solid lines, while the lines separating one province from another are drawn differently — they are not solid.

Hanover is a town in the Northern Cape, while Middelburg is a town in the Eastern Cape.

Describe how the provincial borders are indicated on this map.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: Provincial borders are indicated by a broken line / dotted line / dashed line (2O correct description)

Teaching point: Every map has a KEY (legend) that explains what each type of line means. Borders are almost always drawn as broken/dashed lines so that they can be told apart from roads, rivers and railway lines, which are drawn solid.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Map keys and symbols

subQuestions.questionText:
A flamingo was fitted with a GPS tracking device.

On 13 January 2022, the flamingo was in area A on the map.

On 13 June 2023, it started moving southwards from area A, the starting point of tracking the bird.

Write down the number of months the bird spent in area A.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: 17 months (2A correct number of months)

Teaching point: Count in two blocks. From 13 January 2022 to 13 January 2023 is 12 months; from 13 January 2023 to 13 June 2023 is another 5 months. $12 + 5 = 17$ months. Because both dates fall on the 13th, there are no part-months to worry about.

subQuestions.questionText:
A flamingo fitted with a GPS tracking device followed this path:

- On 13 June 2023 it started moving southwards from area A.
- On 14 June, the flamingo spent the night at a small pan at area B.
- On 15 June at 19:00, it flew non-stop for 14 hours and 25 minutes to arrive at area E, the end point.

Determine the bird's date and time of arrival at area E.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\text{Time of arrival} = 19{:}00 + 14 \text{ hours } 25 \text{ min}$ (1MA adding the flight time)
Mark 2: the date rolls over to 16 June (1A 16 June)
Mark 3: $= 09{:}25$, so the bird arrives on 16 June 2023 at 09:25 (1A arrival time)

OR

Mark 1: From 19:00 to 24:00 is 5 hours (1A 5 hours)
Mark 2: $14 \text{ hours } 25 \text{ min} - 5 \text{ hours} = 9 \text{ hours } 25 \text{ min}$ past midnight, so the date is 16 June (1A 16 June)
Mark 3: arrival at 09:25 → 16 June 2023 at 09:25 (1A arrival time)

Answer only: full marks.

Teaching point: When a journey crosses midnight, split the flight time at 24:00. From 19:00 there are 5 hours left in the day, so the remaining $14\text{h}25 - 5\text{h} = 9\text{h}25$ falls on the NEXT day. Always state the new date as well as the time — a mark is given for it.

subQuestions.questionText:
A road map shows the GPS-tracked flight path of a flamingo from area A (the start), through area B, to area E (the end point). The flight path is drawn as a marked line on the map.

Queenstown is one of the towns printed on the map, but the drawn flight path does NOT pass over Queenstown at any point.

Write down the probability that the bird flew directly over Queenstown.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: 0 ; 0% ; Impossible (2A correct probability)

Teaching point: Probability is always a number from 0 to 1 (or 0% to 100%). An event that CANNOT happen has a probability of exactly 0 and is described as 'impossible'. Since the tracked route never crosses Queenstown, that is what happened here.

subQuestions.questionText:
A flamingo left area B on 15 June at 19:00 and flew non-stop for 14 hours and 25 minutes to arrive at area E.

The flight from area B to area E is 770 km.

Calculate (in km/h) the average speed of the bird as it flew from area B to area E.

You may use this formula: Distance $= \text{speed} \times \text{time}$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $770 \text{ km} = \text{speed} \times 14 \text{ hours } 25 \text{ min}$ (1SF substitution into the formula)
Mark 2: $\text{Speed} = \dfrac{770 \text{ km}}{14 \text{ hours } 25 \text{ min}}$ (1S changing the subject of the formula)
Mark 3: $= \dfrac{770 \text{ km}}{14{,}4166\ldots \text{ hours}}$ (1C converting minutes to hours)
Mark 4: $\approx 53{,}41 \text{ km/h}$ (1CA simplification)

Teaching point: The answer must be in km/h, so the time must be in HOURS — convert the 25 minutes as a fraction of an hour: $25 \div 60 = 0{,}41666\ldots$, giving 14,4166… hours. Typing 14,25 instead of 14,4167 is the most common error here.

subQuestions.questionText:
A flamingo flew from area B to area E, a flight of 770 km.

The direct distance between area B and area E is 311,72 miles.

The person tracking the bird's GPS stated that the bird flew an extra distance of 268,13 km when compared to the direct distance.

1 mile = 1,60934 km

Verify, with calculations, whether this statement is VALID.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $311{,}72 \text{ miles} \times 1{,}60934$ (1MA multiplying by the conversion factor)
Mark 2: $= 501{,}6634\ldots \text{ km}$ (1A simplification)
Mark 3: $\text{Extra distance} = 770 \text{ km} - 501{,}6634\ldots \text{ km}$ (1MCA subtracting)
Mark 4: $= 268{,}336\ldots \text{ km}$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 5: $268{,}34 \text{ km} \neq 268{,}13 \text{ km}$, so the statement is INVALID (1O verification)

OR

Mark 1: $\text{Direct distance} = 311{,}72 \times 1{,}60934 \text{ km}$ (1MA multiplying by 1,60934)
Mark 2: $= 501{,}6634\ldots \text{ km}$ (1A simplification)
Mark 3: $\text{Total distance} = 501{,}6634\ldots \text{ km} + 268{,}13 \text{ km}$ (1MCA adding 268,13)
Mark 4: $= 769{,}7934\ldots \text{ km}$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 5: $769{,}79 \text{ km} \neq 770 \text{ km}$, so the statement is INVALID (1O verification)

Teaching point: 'Verify' means you MUST show the calculation and then write a clear conclusion. Get both distances into the same unit (km) first, then compare. The difference is small (about 0,2 km), but the claim of exactly 268,13 km is still not correct.

subQuestions.questionText:
The biggest flamingo is 59 inches tall, which is approximately 5 feet.

Some interesting facts about a country where flamingos are common:

- Approximately 10% of this country's women are shorter than 5 feet.
- Women make up 50% of this country's population.
- This country has a total population of 333 million people.
- 78% of this country's population are adults.

Calculate, rounded to the nearest million, the number of adult women shorter than 5 feet in this country.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\text{Number of adults} = 78\% \times 333 \text{ million} = 259{,}74 \text{ million}$ (1MA calculating 78%)
Mark 2: $\text{Number of adult women} = 50\% \times 259{,}74 \text{ million} = 129{,}87 \text{ million}$ (1MA calculating 50% of the previous value)
Mark 3: $\text{Number shorter than the flamingo} = 10\% \times 129{,}87 \text{ million}$ (1MA calculating 10% of the previous value)
Mark 4: $= 12{,}987 \text{ million}$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 5: $\approx 13 \text{ million}$ (1R correctly rounded)

OR (percentages applied in the other order)

$\text{Number of women} = 50\% \times 333\,000\,000 = 166\,500\,000$ (1MA calculating 50%)
$\text{Number of adult women} = 78\% \times 166\,500\,000 = 129\,870\,000$ (1MA calculating 78% of the previous value)
$\text{Number shorter} = 10\% \times 129\,870\,000$ (1MA calculating 10% of the previous value)
$= 12\,987\,000$ (1CA simplification)
$\approx 13\,000\,000$ (1R correctly rounded)

Teaching point: This is a chain of percentages — each percentage is worked out on the ANSWER FROM THE PREVIOUS STEP, not on the original 333 million each time. Because multiplication can be done in any order, doing 50% first and 78% second gives exactly the same result.
subQuestions.topic: Finance – Successive percentages of a population

subQuestions.label: 5.1.1 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
Simon is a carpenter. He builds wooden bookcases using wooden pieces for shelves and the frame, and hardboard for the back.

DIAGRAM 1 shows the assembled bookcase: the wooden pieces for the top, bottom, sides and shelves, with the hardboard for the back of the bookcase. The bookcase stands 90 cm high, is 60 cm wide and 20 cm deep. Its two shelves fit BETWEEN the two side pieces.

DIAGRAM 2 shows the hardboard and the SIX pieces of wood, with dimensions, that have to be cut out to assemble a single bookcase:

| Letter in DIAGRAM 2 | Material | Dimensions |
|---|---|---|
| A | wood | 90 cm × 20 cm |
| B | wood | 90 cm × 20 cm |
| C | hardboard | (the large rectangle labelled “Hardboard” — no dimensions are printed on it) |
| D | wood | 60 cm × 20 cm |
| E | wood | 60 cm × 20 cm |
| F | wood | 56 cm × 20 cm |
| G | wood | 56 cm × 20 cm |

Choose the letter (A–G) in DIAGRAM 2 that matches the item in DIAGRAM 1 given below. Write down only the letter.

Shelf
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: F OR G (2RT for the correct letter)

Teaching point: The shelves must fit BETWEEN the two side pieces, so they cannot be the full 60 cm width of the bookcase. Each side piece is 2 cm thick, so the shelf is $60 - 2 - 2 = 56$ cm long. Pieces F and G are the only 56 cm pieces, so either letter is accepted.

subQuestions.questionText:
Simon the carpenter builds a wooden bookcase that is 90 cm high, 60 cm wide and 20 cm deep. TWO shelves are fitted between the top and the bottom of the bookcase, so that the inside of the bookcase is divided into THREE open shelf spaces.

DIAGRAM 1 gives the height of each of the three shelf spaces, measured from the top of the bookcase downwards, as 27 cm, 27 cm and 32 cm.

Write down the probability of randomly placing a book on a shelf with a height greater than 30 cm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: $P = \dfrac{1}{3}$ OR $0{,}333$ OR $33{,}3\%$ (1A numerator; 1A denominator)
No penalty for correct rounding.

Teaching point: Probability $= \dfrac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{total number of outcomes}}$. Here there are 3 shelf spaces altogether (the total) and only 1 of them — the 32 cm space — is higher than 30 cm (the favourable outcome), giving $\frac{1}{3}$. Check the reading: $27 + 27 + 32 = 86$ cm, plus the two 2 cm shelves, gives the 90 cm height of the bookcase.

subQuestions.label: 5.1.3 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
Simon the carpenter builds a wooden bookcase. The bookcase is 90 cm high, 60 cm wide (its length) and 20 cm deep.

The back of the bookcase is made out of hardboard, cut to 60 cm by 90 cm.

Explain why the dimensions of the hardboard is 60 cm by 90 cm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: The length of the bookcase is 60 cm and the height of the bookcase is 90 cm (2O explanation)

OR

It covers the entire back of the bookcase (2O explanation)

Teaching point: The back panel must match the OUTSIDE dimensions of the frame it is nailed to. The face of the bookcase that the back panel covers is a rectangle of 60 cm (width) by 90 cm (height) — the depth of 20 cm plays no part.

subQuestions.label: 5.1.3 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
This is a DRAWING task.

Simon the carpenter builds a wooden bookcase. The back of the bookcase is a rectangular sheet of hardboard measuring 60 cm by 90 cm.

Draw a scaled diagram of the hardboard according to scale 1 : 20.

(Your answer must be a rectangle drawn on paper with a ruler, with the scaled measurements clearly indicated.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Dimensions:
Mark 1: $\text{Width} = 60 \text{ cm} \div 20$ (1MA using the scale)
Mark 2: $= 3 \text{ cm}$ (1A simplification)
Mark 3: $\text{Height} = 90 \text{ cm} \div 20 = 4{,}5 \text{ cm}$ (1CA simplification)

Drawing:
Mark 4: width drawn as 3 cm (1CA width drawn)
Mark 5: height drawn as 4,5 cm (1CA height drawn)
Mark 6: the correct SHAPE drawn — a rectangle, taller than it is wide, with the measurements labelled (1CA shape)

Teaching point: A scale of $1:20$ means every 20 cm of the real object is drawn as 1 cm, so DIVIDE each real measurement by 20. Work out BOTH scaled measurements first, then draw the rectangle accurately with a ruler and label the sides — marks are awarded separately for the calculation and for the drawing.

subQuestions.questionText:
Simon the carpenter builds wooden bookcases. The wooden pieces needed for ONE bookcase are:

| Pieces | Number needed | Dimensions of each |
|---|---|---|
| A and B (sides) | 2 | 90 cm × 20 cm |
| D and E (top and bottom) | 2 | 60 cm × 20 cm |
| F and G (shelves) | 2 | 56 cm × 20 cm |

(The back of the bookcase is hardboard and is NOT cut from this wood.)

The wooden pieces for TWO identical bookcases are cut from ONE complete rectangular piece of wood which is 2 cm thick, 42 cm wide and 430 cm long.

Determine the area of the remaining part of the wood after cutting the required material.

You may use the following formula:

Area of rectangle $= \text{length} \times \text{breadth}$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\text{Area of the complete piece of wood} = 42 \text{ cm} \times 430 \text{ cm}$ (1SF substitution into the formula)
Mark 2: $= 18\,060 \text{ cm}^2$ (1A simplification)
Mark 3: $\text{Area of the pieces of ONE bookcase} = (90 + 60 + 56) \text{ cm} \times (20 + 20) \text{ cm}$ (1MA total length and width)
Mark 4: $= 8\,240 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 5: $\text{Area of unused wood} = 18\,060 - 2(8\,240)$ (1MCA multiplying by 2)
Mark 6: $= 1\,580 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA simplification)

OR (piece by piece)

$\text{Area of complete piece} = 42 \text{ cm} \times 430 \text{ cm} = 18\,060 \text{ cm}^2$ (1SF; 1A)
For 1 bookcase (1MA total length and width):
$\text{Area D \& E} = 60 \text{ cm} \times 20 \text{ cm} \times 2 = 2\,400 \text{ cm}^2$
$\text{Area F \& G} = 56 \text{ cm} \times 20 \text{ cm} \times 2 = 2\,240 \text{ cm}^2$
$\text{Area A \& B} = 90 \text{ cm} \times 20 \text{ cm} \times 2 = 3\,600 \text{ cm}^2$
$\text{Total} = (2\,400 + 2\,240 + 3\,600) \text{ cm}^2 = 8\,240 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA)
For 2 bookcases: $8\,240 \text{ cm}^2 \times 2 = 16\,480 \text{ cm}^2$ (1MCA)
$\text{Remaining} = 18\,060 \text{ cm}^2 - 16\,480 \text{ cm}^2 = 1\,580 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA)

OR (using lengths)

$\text{Total length of the pieces of one bookcase} = 2(90) + 2(60) + 2(56)$ (1MA adding values and multiplying by 2)
$= 412 \text{ cm}$ (1A)
$\text{Wood left over along the length} = 430 \text{ cm} - 412 \text{ cm} = 18 \text{ cm}$ (1MA subtraction; 1CA)
$\text{Area of unused wood} = 18 \text{ cm} \times 40 \text{ cm} + (2 \times 430) = 720 + 860 = 1\,580 \text{ cm}^2$ (1MCA adding unused areas; 1CA)

Teaching point: All six pieces are 20 cm wide, so two bookcases are cut as two strips of 20 cm laid side by side — that uses 40 cm of the 42 cm width and leaves a 2 cm strip running the full 430 cm length. Along each strip the pieces use $90 + 60 + 56 = 206$ cm per bookcase; two bookcases per strip need 412 cm of the 430 cm, leaving an 18 cm off-cut. The 2 cm THICKNESS is not used at all in an area calculation.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Area of rectangles and off-cuts

subQuestions.questionText:
Simon the carpenter is left with unused wood each month.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Density of the wood | 0,75 g/cm³ |
| Volume of unused wood accumulated each month | approximately 0,4 m³ |

Simon states that it will take MORE THAN three months to accumulate one ton of unused wood.

Verify his statement, showing ALL calculations.

You may use the following formula:

Density $= \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}$

(Note: 1 ton = 1 000 kg and 1 kg = 1 000 g.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\text{Volume of wood per month} = 0{,}4 \text{ m}^3 \times 100^3 = 400\,000 \text{ cm}^3$ (1C converting m³ to cm³)
Mark 2: $\text{Mass per month} = 0{,}75 \text{ g/cm}^3 \times 400\,000 \text{ cm}^3$ (1MA substitution)
Mark 3: $= 300\,000 \text{ g}$ (1CA mass in grams)
Mark 4: $300\,000 \text{ g} \div 1\,000 = 300 \text{ kg}$, and $1 \text{ ton} = 1\,000 \text{ kg}$ (1C tonnes to kg)
Mark 5: $\text{Number of months} = 1\,000 \text{ kg} \div 300 \text{ kg} = 3{,}33$ (1CA number of months)
Mark 6: $3{,}33 > 3$, so his statement is VALID (1O verification)

OR

$\text{Unused wood per month} = (0{,}4 \times 1\,000\,000) \text{ cm}^3 \times 0{,}75 \text{ g/cm}^3$ (1MA substitution; 1C conversion)
$= 300\,000 \text{ g}$ (1CA mass in grams)
$= 300 \text{ kg} = 0{,}3 \text{ ton}$ (1C converting to tonnes)
$\text{Tons in 3 months} = 0{,}3 \times 3 = 0{,}9 \text{ ton}$ (1CA)
$0{,}9 \text{ ton} < 1 \text{ ton}$, so his statement is VALID (1O verification)

OR

$0{,}4 \text{ m}^3 \times 3 = 1{,}2 \text{ m}^3$ in 3 months (1A volume in 3 months)
$\text{Mass} = (1{,}2 \times 100 \times 100 \times 100 \times 0{,}75) \text{ g}$ (1MA substitution; 1C converting m³ to cm³)
$= 900\,000 \text{ g}$ (1CA mass in g)
$= 900 \text{ kg}$ (1C converting to kg for 3 months)
$900 \text{ kg} < 1\,000 \text{ kg}$, so his statement is correct — VALID (1O verification)

Teaching point: For VOLUME conversions the factor is cubed: $1 \text{ m}^3 = 100 \times 100 \times 100 = 1\,000\,000 \text{ cm}^3$. Then $\text{mass} = \text{density} \times \text{volume}$. Because only 300 kg builds up each month, three months gives 900 kg — still short of a ton — so it really does take more than three months.
